children.translated_text: Obeisance to <s>Śiva</s> and to <s>Śakti</s>,
to <s>Bindu</s> and to the eternal one,
to the <s>Guru</s> and to <s>Gaṇeśa</s>,
to the wise <s>Kārtikeya</s>.
The three [jewels] called <s>Bindu</s>, <s>Śakti</s>, and <s>Śiva</s>,
extracted from the ocean of <s>Siddhānta</s>,
in order to hold [them] always for the good,
in heart, throat, and ears—
these jewels are strung by me
with verbal threads; therefore
may the saints forgive [any fault],
[and show] no jealousy toward [this] servant.
Because of delighting in all <s>tattvas</s> (principles),
and because of [conferring] attachment and authority
upon the <s>Īśvaras</s> (lords) and <s>Śivas</s>,
because of being worthy of being held in the mind,
and because of [possessing] an irresistible, noble
host of rays for [all] beings,
and because of bestowing what is desired—
<s>Bindu</s> and the rest [are called jewels] in the <s>Śiva-śāsana</s> (teaching of Śiva).
Depending on the <s>Ratnatraya</s> (three jewels),
the aggregate of <s>tattvas</s> (principles) operates;
the <s>adhvan</s> (path) is attained through them in six ways,
as described by the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameṣṭhin</s>).
This very doctrine is the seed—
the triad—of <s>dīkṣā</s> (initiation) and <s>pratiṣṭhā</s> (consecration),
and the various <s>yogas</s>, and <s>karma</s> (ritual action)
both <s>nitya</s> (daily) and <s>naimittika</s> (occasional).
The [various] knowledges, <s>siddhis</s> (supernatural attainments), and <s>mokṣas</s> (liberations)
also [arise] from the understanding of that [triad].
This alone is the supreme limit,
called <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), upon investigation of the souls (<s>aṇus</s>).
This should be heard from the authoritative statement (<s>āptokti</s>),
reflected upon with reasonings,
and meditated upon through the path of <s>yoga</s>,
by those whose selves have been awakened by the descent of <s>Śakti</s> (<s>śaktipāta</s>).
The authoritative statement here is the <s>Siddhānta</s>,
since <s>Śiva</s> alone is the authoritative one (<s>āpta</s>),
for there is no one comparable to those two [<s>Śiva</s> and <s>Siddhānta</s>]
who is a bestower of the highest good and [who is truly] authoritative.
<s>Siddhānta</s> alone is the [true] <s>Siddhānta</s>;
the other [systems] are therefore merely <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (preliminary positions).
The [truly] authoritative one is <s>Śiva</s> alone;
those other than <s>Śiva</s> are considered <s>aśiva</s> (non-auspicious).
<s>Siddhānta</s> is served by the good,
who are purified by <s>śaktipāta</s> (descent of grace);
but by others, acting as they please,
it is disparaged, like a scripture for beasts (<s>paśu</s>).
The fragrance of musk
is not repelled by men;
nor is it proved by arguments—rather,
it is always smelled by the fortunate.
By <s>Vedāntas</s> and <s>Kulāmnāyas</s> (tantric lineage scriptures),
and by others too, what is taught is
consciousness endowed with bliss—
for those deluded about [true] bliss.
The depth of the great ocean of consciousness
could be ascertained by the wise,
if the wave of supreme bliss
did not toss [them] up.
Therefore, all this has been declared
in the greatest of the streams of the Lord,
by the upward-facing mouth from the north;
therefore one should ascertain that.
One should also note the logical reasons
for the sake of examination, from that scripture;
for here, even pure intellect,
however vast, does not dare [to proceed independently].
Supramundane, subtle,
and concealed by <s>Śiva</s>—
who knows the three jewels
by themselves, without the <s>Siddhānta</s>?
And who knows the logical reasons too,
which destroy the darkness of sophistry,
through [mere] reflection? And likewise, who knows <s>yoga</s>,
characterized as <s>sabīja</s> (with seed) and <s>abīja</s> (without seed)?
<s>Siddhānta</s>, when served by the good,
also grants all desires
that are present in the mind of the practitioner—
the authoritative [source], like a <s>Cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-fulfilling jewel).
Having resorted to that [<s>Siddhānta</s>], by me too this
examination (<s>parīkṣā</s>), based on <s>Bindu</s>, <s>Śakti</s>, and <s>Śiva</s>,
is undertaken; therein,
<s>Bindu</s> is examined first.
That from which the pure path (<s>adhvan</s>) arises,
in which it exists, and into which it dissolves—
that is <s>Bindu</s>, called <s>Paranāda</s> (supreme sound),
the cause of <s>Nāda</s>, <s>Bindu</s>, and <s>Varṇa</s> (phoneme).
Having crossed the ocean of <s>Māyā</s>,
having broken the great bolt of <s>karma</s>,
[yet] not having attained the abode of <s>Śiva</s>—
the <s>Vijñānakevalas</s> (souls with knowledge alone) are threefold.
Lords of <s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance),
preceded by <s>Paśus</s> (bound souls), [up to] <s>Sadāśivas</s>—
among them, the first are those who partake of <s>Vidyā</s>,
called <s>Mantras</s> and <s>Vidyās</s> by name.
They are to be employed by the <s>Vidyeśvaras</s>;
in number, they are seventy million.
Their cities [are situated] in <s>Vidyā</s>,
beginning with <s>Vāmā</s> and so forth, in order.
Nine [cities] arose, expanded
with bodies, experiences, senses, and the like.
The middle [class] are the <s>Vidyeśvaras</s> (lords of knowledge),
whose impurities are pacified, [endowed with] the splendor of <s>Śiva</s>,
possessed of the <s>mala</s> (impurity) of [limited] authority,
abiding in the <s>Aiśa-tattva</s> (the principle of the Lord),
whose own powers have blossomed
through contact with the rays of <s>Śiva</s>, the sun.
They are eight, preceded by <s>Ananta</s>,
each succeeding one having greater qualities.
Their cities likewise [are there];
among them, <s>Ananta</s> is the supreme lord.
In those cities were <s>aṇus</s> (bound souls),
and also others who are his manifestations.
The last [class] are those equal to <s>Sadāśiva</s>,
who are authorized for the functions of the Lord (<s>Pati</s>).
They have reached the summit of the path,
when the Supreme Lord is pleased.
Their <s>tattva</s> (principle), adorned with limbs,
cities, experiences, and the like,
is <s>Sadāśiva</s>; by the name of their presiding deity,
they too are [called] <s>Sadāśivas</s>.
With eighteen <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds),
along with their experiencers,
and with three <s>tattvas</s> (principles), this path is described
as pure, with <s>Śiva</s> as the agent.
The aggregate of <s>tattvas</s> beginning with <s>Sadāśiva</s>
is the eternal material cause.
Because it is subject to modification, like a pot—
and so this [aggregate is] likewise from that [cause].
Even though a pot is of earth,
<s>Māyā</s> is the material cause [of the impure path].
Because of possessing destruction and origination,
and because of being subject to transformation—
whatever entity arises,
that belongs to <s>Māyā</s>, like <s>Kalā</s>.
Origination and destruction are properties
belonging to the domain of <s>Māyā</s>—so declared the Great Lord.
For transformation of things
is the departure from a prior state
and the attainment of another state,
like milk becoming curd,
and curd becoming buttermilk. Therein,
the state of buttermilk is to be examined:
it is neither the prior state of curd
nor that of milk—for those are considered [different] states.
But it is one substance that is always in some state—
first milk, then curd,
and afterwards buttermilk. Similarly, <s>Māyā</s>,
through its manifold transformations,
is the imperishable material cause
of <s>tattvas</s> (principles) and the states of those tattvas.
Therefore, the illustration is fitting,
characterized as is well known.
Neither <s>Māyā</s>, nor <s>Īśvara</s>, nor the <s>aṇu</s> (soul),
nor <s>Śakti</s> [is the material cause] of the pure path.
Therefore, <s>Bindu</s> is obtained
as the material cause, by elimination.
For that <s>Māyā</s> which, among them,
agitated by the power of <s>Ananta</s>,
produced the entire class of <s>tattvas</s>
from water up to earth—
because of being impure and insentient,
because of being the path of <s>Māyā</s>,
because of the connection with suffering, because of
the association with <s>māyīya</s>, <s>kārma</s>, and <s>āṇava</s> impurities,
because of being the object of experience for all bound souls,
and because of the arising of transformations—
<s>Māyā</s>, pervaded by insentient [substance] within,
and being subject to transformation,
in the production of <s>Kalā</s> and the other [tattvas],
endowed with body and the rest,
would surely lead the <s>puruṣa</s> (soul)
to a state of dependence—without doubt—
like gold [leading] the goldsmith
in the work of producing a crown.
This very [<s>Māyā</s>], being within the range
of determinate cognition (<s>vikalpa-vijñāna</s>),
is agitated by <s>Ananta</s>, the lord,
just as clay [is shaped] by a potter.
Determinate cognition (<s>savikalpaka-vijñāna</s>)
arises from the penetration of word (<s>śabda</s>) into consciousness (<s>cit</s>).
That word (<s>śabda</s>) is fourfold: speech (<s>vāc</s>),
by the division into <s>Vaikharī</s> and the others.
It arises from the agitation of <s>Bindu</s>,
when <s>Ananta</s> perceives objects.
The Lord <s>Ananta</s>, whose body is <s>Vidyā</s>,
is regarded as the agitator
of <s>Māyā</s>; and that [body] is called
by the learned the <s>Baindava-tattva</s> (principle pertaining to <s>Bindu</s>).
Therefore <s>Māyā</s> is not the material cause;
likewise this <s>Maheśvara</s> (Great Lord) [is not either].
Because of being conscious, because of not undergoing modification,
and because of transformation—therefore,
the <s>Ātman</s> (self) and <s>Śakti</s> should be understood [as not being the material cause];
the elaboration will be stated here itself.
Moreover, <s>Bindu</s> is also inferred
from the observation of inequality among souls.
Some individuals are seen
to possess little knowledge and action;
others superior to them, and yet others
are omniscient and powerful.
The individual soul (<s>pudgala</s>) is conscious, eternal,
and considered free from modification.
If it were subject to modification, there would be
insentience and non-eternality, like a pot or a wall.
Likewise <s>Citi</s> (consciousness-power), which is <s>Śakti</s>—
for both of these, which are unmodifiable,
the manifold state of existence
would be due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>).
That by which the <s>cit</s> (consciousness) of the soul, when conjoined,
[engages] in the perception of objects from <s>Māyā</s> onwards,
and by whose limiting adjunct it becomes variegated—
that is <s>Bindu</s>, having many modes.
<s>Karma</s> alone, without [<s>Bindu</s>],
does not produce diversity for the soul.
Even the diversity of experience
is [produced] only by [<s>karma</s>] dependent [on co-factors].
<s>Karma</s> brings about the experience;
sandal-paste and other [accessories bring about] the diversity.
If that [<s>karma</s>] alone could produce that [diversity],
what would be the use of those? Let them be dispensed with.
The activity of all beings
is the cause of renunciation and appropriation.
Moreover, [the sages] declare that which is supremely transcendent,
that [supreme] space (<s>ambara</s>), imperishable—
for the <s>Śivas</s> of unequal sovereignty,
in both experience and authority,
like space for the luminaries,
is the cause, being the source of the elements and the rest.
<s>Bindu</s> alone, in determinate cognitions,
characterized as conceptual determination (<s>vikalpa</s>),
by the combinations of its own diverse modes,
inscribing [the content], attains consciousness.
And this is not a mental impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>)
called a latent impression (<s>bhāvanā</s>), because it is of the nature of direct experience.
For mental impressions are indicated by memory
and are not within the range of our direct perception.
Nor is it a transformation of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect),
since [determinate cognition] occurs even above <s>Māyā</s>.
Thus <s>Vidyeśvara</s> <s>Ananta</s>,
invading <s>Māyā</s> with [his] power,
then carries out creation,
possessing determinate knowledge.
Being an <s>aṇu</s> (limited soul) yet having agency,
like a servant commissioned by us.
Others, skilled in the doctrines distinguishing
between <s>vṛtti</s> (modification) and <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation),
the teachers explain this [<s>Bindu</s>]
with different characterization.
This [<s>Bindu</s>] is the agent of transformation,
but not of modification; therefore, accordingly,
'This, agitated by me in this way,
will certainly produce what is desired'—
one who knows thus and is capable,
he is the agent of transformable things.
This property [of agenthood] in transformable things
would be otherwise in things subject to modification.
For indeed, everyone, observing
a thing free from conceptual determination,
the world cognizes [it] as the object,
and then differently as a determinate [cognition].
Even by <s>Ananta</s>, preceded by cognition
pervaded by word (<s>śabda</s>),
if all here is cognized—
it is accepted that he also acts.
'I cognize determinately'—
from the self-awareness of knowing,
the <s>vṛtti</s> (modification) of <s>Bindu</s> is recognized,
like [the modification of] cloth into a tent. Therefore,
even in indeterminate cognition,
<s>Īśa</s> (the Lord) presides over <s>Bindu</s>.
But the <s>Vidyeśvara</s> does not thus [preside over] <s>Māyā</s>,
for this [<s>Māyā</s>] is subject to transformation [not modification].
The distinction of the agent is not ascertained
from [the distinction between] <s>vṛtti</s> and <s>pariṇāma</s>.
Even for one making a tent,
determinate cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is indeed seen.
The <s>śabda-tattva</s> (principle of sound), unvocalized speech (<s>aghoṣā vāc</s>),
<s>Brahman</s>, <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>, the eternal [one],
<s>Vidyā-śakti</s>, the supreme, <s>Nāda</s>,
<s>Mahāmāyā</s>—by the teachers,
<s>Bindu</s> has been designated thus,
and also as <s>Vyoman</s> (space) and <s>Anāhata</s> (unstruck [sound]).
Its four <s>vṛttis</s> (modes),
by which the souls (<s>aṇus</s>) are pervaded in three ways, are:
<s>Vaikharī</s>, that called <s>Madhyamā</s>,
<s>Paśyantī</s>, and that named <s>Sūkṣmā</s> (subtle).
Among these, <s>Vaikharī</s> is that [speech] which,
graspable by the ear, is the verbal [expression] of meaning,
when breath is held at the [articulatory] places
and phonemes (<s>varṇas</s>) are formed.
This [<s>Vaikharī</s>], for speakers, is mostly
dependent on the activity of <s>prāṇa</s> (breath).
Solely arising from the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>),
following phonemes in sequence,
having the nature of inner silent speech,
[<s>Madhyamā</s>] does not reach the ear.
Transcending the activity of <s>prāṇa</s>,
it operates—[this] is called <s>Madhyamā</s>.
Without differentiation of phonemes,
with the sequence entirely withdrawn,
self-luminous—<s>Paśyantī</s>
is like the fluid inside a peacock's egg.
The inner light of one's own nature—
the subtle (<s>Sūkṣmā</s>) speech, imperishable;
when her true nature is beheld,
[the soul's] authority [over worldly affairs] ceases.

children.translated_text: In the <s>puruṣa</s> (person) with sixteen <s>kalās</s>,
they call her by the name 'immortal' (<s>amṛtā</s>).
The solitary one, [whose nature is] supreme bliss,
the awesome (<s>ghora</s>) [one], eternally arisen, the lord—
neither sets nor rises,
neither tires nor changes—
moving within all beings,
the sun (<s>ravi</s>) whose nature is <s>Śabda-brahman</s> (the Absolute as Word).
Piercing through whom with the sword of knowledge,
[yogins] go forth without hesitation—
that very speech called <s>Sūkṣmā</s> (subtle),
those who know the Self declare.
These <s>vṛttis</s> (modes), specific to each individual self,
are of the nature of bondage.
Individuals (<s>pudgalas</s>) do not see the self
as distinct from these [modes].
'The Supreme Self is the essence of speech;
speech alone is the Self'—thus from scripture.
<s>Vaikharī</s> is [perceived] in auditory cognition;
<s>Madhyamā</s> in determinate [cognition].
<s>Paśyantī</s> is perceived in the impulses
that give rise to <s>Madhyamā</s>.
When the function [of speech] has completely
dissolved, resting in consciousness—
then <s>Sūkṣmā</s> (the subtle), being pure,
appears as consciousness (<s>cit</s>) itself, due to non-discrimination.
There is no cognition of the souls (<s>aṇus</s>)
that arises without the accompaniment of word (<s>śabda</s>).
All knowledge here arises
pervaded by word (<s>śabda</s>).

children.translated_text: This very fourfold <s>vṛtti</s> (mode),
due to resting upon <s>kalās</s> beginning with <s>Nivṛtti</s>,
is further divided into five;
those <s>kalās</s> are the modes of <s>Bindu</s>.
<s>Nivṛtti</s>, <s>Pratiṣṭhā</s>,
<s>Vidyā</s>, <s>Śānti</s>, and the fifth,
<s>Śāntyatītā</s>—these are the <s>kalās</s>,
by which the fivefold <s>adhvan</s> (path) is pervaded.
The <s>tattva-adhvan</s> (path of principles), the <s>bhuvana-adhvan</s> (path of worlds),
the <s>varṇa-adhvan</s> (path of phonemes), and that consisting of <s>padas</s> (words),
the <s>mantra-adhvan</s> (path of mantras)—the all-pervading among these
is the <s>kalā-adhvan</s> (path of kalās), which depends on <s>Bindu</s>.
Leaving one after another and reaching [the next],
in the <s>kalās</s> and the rest, the imperishable and ageless
state is attained by souls;
therefore, the <s>kalās</s> and the rest are [called] <s>adhvans</s> (paths).
The <s>kalā-adhvan</s> has been described previously
with the divisions of <s>Nivṛtti</s> and the rest.
I shall describe its pervasion—
with its supports, emblems, and presiding deities,
with its forms and causes, resting upon
<s>Ātman</s> (self), <s>Bindu</s>, <s>Śakti</s>, and <s>Śiva</s>.
In <s>Nivṛtti</s>, the earthly (<s>pārthiva</s>) <s>tattva</s> (principle) [resides];
the worlds (<s>purāṇi</s>) number one hundred and eight.
Among them, beginning with <s>Kālānala</s> (the fire of time) and the rest,
six are outside the egg of <s>Ananta</s>.
In the eastern and other directions, in the ten
quarters, ten in each,
[are the worlds] of the hundred <s>Rudras</s>,
and above [them, the world] of <s>Vīrabhadra</s>,
and the world of <s>Bhadrakālī</s>.
The phoneme <s>kṣa</s> is declared among the <s>varṇas</s> (letters).

children.translated_text: The goddess with eighty-one <s>padas</s> (words/stations)
in the order of dissolution.
With twenty-eight
words (<s>padas</s>), it is established here.
The two <s>mantras</s> are <s>Aja</s> and <s>Hṛdaya</s>;
there, that is the supreme <s>kalā</s>.
Pervading the <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds) and the rest,
five [kalās] abide in five [groups].
She is yellow, quadrangular,
hard, and marked with the <s>vajra</s> (thunderbolt).
She is to be meditated upon as having many rising rays,
fleshy, in the lotus of the heart.
For the group of <s>aṇus</s> (souls) dissolved therein,
volition ceases.
Because of not attaining the fruit, therefore
it is called <s>Nivṛtti</s> (cessation).
<s>Brahmā</s> is the cause here; the <s>mantra</s>
is <s>Sadyojāta</s>; [he is] the presiding deity.
In the <s>Pratiṣṭhā</s> <s>kalā</s>, four
[kalās exist]; excluding earth,
the five elements, the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements),
the five organs of action,
the five organs of knowledge,
mind, ego, and intellect,
and also the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>); and the phonemes
from 'ha' to the end of the 'ṭa' group, in reverse order.
Twenty-three are taught;
and fifty-six <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds).
In water, fire, wind, space,
intellect, the unmanifest, and ego —
eight and eight <s>padas</s> (words), and one
twenty — that is the count there.
The two <s>mantras</s> are <s>Śiras</s> (head) and <s>Vāma</s>;
<s>Viṣṇu</s> is declared as the cause.
She is white, resembling a half-moon,
adorned with a blue lotus petal;
she is to be meditated upon within the lotus of the throat,
resplendent with abundant radiance.
For the group of <s>aṇus</s> (souls) dissolved therein,
volition, for the accomplishment of objects,
is established; therefore,
that <s>kalā</s> is called <s>Pratiṣṭhā</s> (establishment).
<s>Vāmadeva</s> is indeed the presider;
the expressed [deity] is considered to be of the nature of <s>mantra</s>.
In <s>Vidyā</s>, seven [tattvas]: <s>puruṣa</s>,
<s>rāga</s> (attachment), together with <s>niyati</s> (destiny),
<s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), <s>kalā</s> (limited agency), <s>kāla</s> (time),
and <s>Māyā</s> — [these are] the <s>tattvas</s> there.
And of the <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds) beginning with <s>Māyā</s>,
twenty-seven should be known.
Here the phonemes are from 'ña' onward,
ending with 'gha' — seven, in reverse order.

children.text: i.e. gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, and ña in vidyākalā

children.translated_text: The <s>padas</s> (words) are twenty; the two <s>mantras</s>
established are <s>Śikhā</s> (topknot) and <s>Aghora</s>.
<s>Rudra</s> is the cause here; the <s>mantra</s>
has <s>Bahurūpa</s> (many-formed) as presiding deity.
She blazes with many rays,
is triangular, and marked with the <s>svastika</s>.
She is to be meditated upon within the lotus of the palate,
having the splendor of dark collyrium.
For the group of <s>aṇus</s> (souls) dissolved therein,
volition encompasses all objects;
because it illuminates all meanings,
therefore it is celebrated as <s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge).
In <s>Śānti</s>, three <s>tattvas</s>
and eighteen <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds)
are declared; and the phonemes here
are considered to be three, from 'ga' to 'ka.'

children.text: i.e. ka, kha, and ga; in śāntikalā

children.translated_text: The <s>padas</s> are eleven here;
the two <s>mantras</s> are <s>Vaktra</s> (face) and <s>Tanucchada</s> (body-concealing).
Pervading the <s>bhuvanas</s> and the rest,
five [kalās exist], marked with six <s>bindus</s> (dots),
with the splendor of a thousand rays
arising from a hexagon, ending with 'ma.'
She, the supreme <s>Śakti</s>, is to be meditated upon
in the interior of the lotus between the eyebrows.
For the group of <s>aṇus</s> dissolved therein,
due to the absence of hatred, passion, and the like,
because of the pacification of volition,
this [kalā] is called <s>Śānti</s> (tranquility).
<s>Īśvara</s> is the cause there;
the <s>mantra</s> is named <s>Tatpuruṣa</s>.
The presider of that should be known;
<s>Puruṣa</s> is the presiding deity.
And here, three <s>tattvas</s>;
the fifth is the supreme <s>kalā</s>.
There, the <s>Śiva-tattva</s> (Śiva-principle)
and fifteen <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds).
The phonemes preceded by <s>visarga</s>,
sixteen in number, designated as vowels.

body.text: i.e.: a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ = all vowels in śāntyatītakalā

children.translated_text: '<s>Oṃ</s>' is the first <s>pada</s> (word); the <s>mantras</s>
are called <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Astra</s> (weapon), and <s>Īśāna</s>.
<s>Śāntyatītā</s> (that which transcends tranquility), containing the five <s>adhvans</s> (paths),
is the supreme <s>kalā</s>.
She is to be contemplated as having the nature
of the great space, in the lotus of the crown.
<s>Īśāna</s> is the king of <s>mantras</s>;
he presides over her; the cause
is the god <s>Sadāśiva</s> there.
This is declared as the <s>kalā-adhvan</s> (path of kalās),
pervading the <s>bhuvanas</s> and the rest;
it is pervaded by <s>Bindu</s>.
<s>Bindu</s> [is pervaded] by <s>Śakti</s>; she by <s>Śiva</s>;
<s>Śiva</s> is not pervaded by any other.
For that God, having encompassed [all]
by his own <s>Śakti</s>, which is non-different [from him],
pervading everything with her,
knows and acts.
The existence of one thing in another,
always without deviation —
that is <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion), the ground for obtaining,
reaching, and sustaining the object [pervaded].
It is twofold: one [operates] by mere proximity,
by the ordainment of the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self).
There, by mere proximity,
consciousness (<s>citi</s>) effects everything —
just as the sun, by its proximity,
is the facilitator of daytime activities.
<s>Bindu</s>, upon the <s>Ātman</s> (Self), the <s>Nāda</s> and the rest —
the six <s>adhvans</s> (paths), in sequence,
through those various transformations,
effects [all], impelled by <s>Śiva</s> —
just as clay [produces] pots and the like
when presided over by the potter.
That entity by which another entity is pervaded
by way of transformation [of the pervading entity itself],
that is called the modification of the former —
just as a crown is [a modification] of gold.
That sixfold <s>adhvan</s> beginning with the <s>kalās</s>
which is pervaded by <s>Bindu</s> —
that is its modification; therefore,
it is pervaded like <s>Nāda</s> by <s>Bindu</s>.
Some say that <s>Bindu</s>
is inherent in <s>Śiva</s>; therefore,
like the power of sight, the power of action —
this supreme <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>.
Two powers are inherent
in <s>Śiva</s>: those of knowledge and action.
The first is consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>), cognition;
action is the supreme <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>.
Through the power of knowledge, he knows;
through action, he creates the universe.
For action alone bestows fruit upon persons;
knowledge would not be a bestower of fruit.
He is never separated from those two,

children.text: te ca na staḥ śivaṃ vinā
children.translated_text: and those two do not exist without <s>Śiva</s>.
When those two flow forth in equal measure,
the <s>tattva</s>-nature becomes <s>Sadāśiva</s>.
When the power of action exceeds that of <s>Īśa</s> (Lord),
and the power of knowledge exceeds that of <s>Vidyā</s>,
in those <s>tattvas</s>, for the
<s>vijñānakevalas</s> (souls with pure knowledge alone), the great selves,
various <s>bhuvanas</s> (worlds),
naturally beautiful companions,
unfading enjoyments,
limbs, and faculties —
<s>Śiva</s> creates [all these] from <s>Śakti</s>,
which is non-different [from him] and of the nature of action.
By that, he is also the creator of <s>Nāda</s> and the rest;
he is considered the maker of the pure path.
Therefore, he is not separate from <s>Śakti</s>;
<s>Śakti</s> itself, of the nature of action,
inherent in <s>Śiva</s>, is <s>Bindu</s> —
thus it is stated there.
He, upon the Self, the mass of <s>tattvas</s>,
the series of many <s>bhuvanas</s>,
producing the various and abundant
bodies, enjoyments, sense organs, and the like —
<s>Bindu</s> is rightly designated
as transformative, like <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter).
And whatever entity undergoes transformation,
that is necessarily of insentient nature —
like milk. If it is insentient,
how can it be inherent in <s>Śiva</s>?
For that relation of identity (<s>tādātmya</s>)
with the insentient would bring insentience [to Śiva].
For <s>Śiva</s>, whose nature is incomparable, undivided,
a solid mass of consciousness alone —
whoever, through delusion, considers
with insentient mind the Lord to be insentient,
for him there is neither reasoning nor scripture,
neither the Self nor any deity.
He should be shunned by the wise,
excluded from all established [doctrines].
Because [<s>Śakti</s>] is the cause through action,
and the power of action is consciousness itself —
<s>Bindu</s> is nothing other [than consciousness]; above <s>Māyā</s>,
there exists no insentient [entity]; therefore it is conscious.
Whence would the pure path arise?
Where would it dissolve, and by what?
How would this [path] become sixfold
through the divisions of <s>tattvas</s>, <s>bhuvanas</s>, and the rest?
The <s>vijñānakevalas</s> (souls with pure knowledge) are of three kinds;
how [do they differ], from what, and moreover,
how would they be liberated, without <s>Bindu</s>
which ordains that variety?
For consciousness does not, by transformation,
produce all of that;
'Because of the nature of consciousness' — this
will be stated later in the investigation of <s>Śakti</s>.

body.text:
Agh: sādhitaṃ cāsmābhistattvaprakāśavṛttau vistareṇa
 The commentary on this work postdates tattvaprakāśavṛtti

children.translated_text: This [Bindu] may be one with fabricated
manifold divisions arising from the variety of effects;
if [one holds that] <s>Śiva</s> is one alone, not
endowed with many powers — if such is the view,
[then] the path belonging to <s>Māyā</s> would be just so,
since there is no difference in reasoning.
The pure paths, established
by their respective proofs — scriptures
and also the direct perception of yogins —
how could a wise person deny them?
When the distinguished, supremely generous
Lord bestows according to scripture,
activity is declared to be for enjoyment
and for liberation.
The state of <s>Sadāśiva</s> is attained
through <s>yoga</s>, conduct (<s>caryā</s>), or <s>dīkṣā</s> (initiation);
through the distinction of mental [attainment],
or liberation from all four [means].

body.text: N.B. This is a quotation of Mat VP 26:63

children.translated_text: Thus, enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) has been declared
as the great state of <s>Sadāśiva</s>.
There, no body or enjoyment arises
with <s>Māyā</s> as material cause,
because of its purity; therefore, the pure path
is established for [their] enjoyment.
Moreover, <s>Māyā</s>, presided over by
some agent who is instrumental,
is the material cause of the <s>kalās</s> and the rest,
having the nature of being pervaded by the <s>kalās</s>.
Just as clay [is the material cause] of pots and the like
[when presided over] by the potter, so too she
[is presided over by] the agent who, being in the state of a <s>paśu</s> (bound soul),
is instrumental; the cause is the great Lord.
The soul (<s>jantu</s>) is declared to be unknowing and powerless
even in matters concerning itself.

 ajño janturanīśo 'yamātmanaḥ sukhaduḥkhayoḥ | īśvaraprerito gacchet svargaṃ vā śvabhrameva vā || 63 ||

 which is quoted in Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha under śaivadarśanam

 Cf. also Pauṣkara 1:86:

children.translated_text: Impelled by the Lord, it performs
either auspicious or inauspicious [deeds].
Because of being instrumental, <s>Ananta</s>,
endowed with body and the like, is like the potter.
He by whom <s>Māyā</s> is agitated,
and through body and sense organs,
and through space and the like — that path is established
as pure, in the teaching of <s>Śiva</s>.
Others, the learned, call <s>Māyā</s>
a state of <s>Bindu</s>;
and because it has the nature of being pervaded by the <s>kalās</s>
and is presided over by individual souls,
it is their <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) as well.
She, being gross, subtle, and supreme,
this <s>Mahāmāyā</s> (great illusion) is threefold.
Among these, the gross one is of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
the <s>Prakṛti</s> of <s>Puruṣa</s> that generates
the objects of enjoyment such as intellect and the rest.
The subtle one, of the nature of non-differentiation
of the <s>tattvas</s> beginning with <s>kalā</s>,
is the generating, deluding <s>Māyā</s>,
the cause of the entire impure path.
The supreme <s>Māyā</s>, the source of <s>mantras</s>,
the eternal <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>,
is the material cause of the bodies
of <s>Vidyās</s> (knowledge-deities) and <s>Vidyeśvaras</s> (lords of knowledge).
Because this <s>Māyā</s> is of the nature of effects
and undergoes transformation,
it would produce an agent endowed with
body and sense organs; therefore,
the establishment of the pure path
stands irrefutably.
For those in whose view <s>Māyā</s> is non-eternal
and the cause of <s>kalā</s>, <s>vidyā</s>, and the rest,
for them, the impure path
is not purified by the purification of the <s>kalās</s>.
For the five <s>kalās</s> — <s>Nivṛtti</s> and the rest —
have been purified for the purification
of the <s>tattvas</s> and the rest; therefore, the path
is specifically an effect of <s>Bindu</s>.
Purification of the paths is not accepted
through the purification of mere pervaders
that are not in the form of material causes;
for the <s>kalās</s>, which are eternally pure —
[belong to] <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Śakti</s>, and by their purity alone
there would always be the undesirable consequence of [universal] purification.
Thus has been declared <s>Mahāmāyā</s>,
the supreme source of all paths.
By those teachers who are experts
in the doctrine that all paths are effects [of Bindu].
Others, however, declare here
that <s>Māyā</s> is imperishable in the paths,
is the material cause of the <s>kalās</s> and the rest,
and is pervaded by <s>Bindu</s>.
And such purification should be known
by those two [groups of teachers] who know the <s>Āgamas</s> —
that by which, through the purification of the pervader alone,
the purification of the rest that depends [on it follows].
The <s>Mahāmāyā</s>, the source of <s>mantras</s>,
which abides in possession [of the Lord],
the <s>Śakti</s> of <s>Śiva</s>, pervaded
by which are all individual souls —
this is the power of action, the sovereign goddess,
ever-risen,
abiding in the <s>paśus</s> (bound souls) themselves,
established in the form of bonds (<s>pāśa</s>).
She perpetually causes the <s>paśus</s> to revolve
in various wombs, without certainty,
and through the power of self-reflection,
bestows enjoyment and liberation.
She, through the arising of the means and conditions
for the instruments of enjoyment,
always deludes through the pervading of <s>śabda</s> (word),
when not discriminated.
In every way extending the separation
from the attainment of <s>amṛta</s> (immortality),
therefore, for those whose minds are eager
and delighted by the enjoyment of sense-objects,
the knowledge that is the means to the supreme <s>amṛta</s>
becomes the equipment of the <s>paśu</s> (bound soul).
And that, through the pervading of <s>śabda</s>,
arose from the mass of words.
And the mass of words arose from <s>Bindu</s>;
<s>Bindu</s> arose from <s>Nāda</s>.
And <s>Bindu</s>, from <s>Anāhata</s> (the unstruck) —
this is the cause of the pure path.
There, through experiencership, through enjoyments
pertaining to body and sense organs,
<s>mala</s> (impurity), <s>karma</s>, and <s>Māyā</s>
are inferred as pure [in the pure path].
Pure <s>Māyā</s> alone is the cause
of the pure [forms of] <s>mala</s> and <s>karma</s>;
of the impure [forms], impure <s>Māyā</s> alone [is the cause];
therefore <s>Māyā</s> is considered twofold.
Upon the discrimination of <s>Bindu</s>,
the shell (<s>kambuka</s>) of <s>mala</s> is suddenly cut.
Upon the discrimination of <s>Māyā</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>,
there is the destruction of the husk of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit).
Directing [its activity] toward the self
that has transcended <s>Māyā</s> but is still connected with <s>Mahāmāyā</s>,
the <s>Śakti</s> of the Lord
operates for the agitation of <s>Bindu</s>.
Just as the ocean transforms
only on its surface from the agitation of wind,
so <s>Bindu</s> [transforms] in one part;
and [<s>Śakti</s>] pervades the whole through <s>Śakti</s>.
Likewise, <s>Māyā</s>, by a portion,
transforms; and the whole
pervades its own effect;
likewise, the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>) is regarded [similarly].
When <s>Bindu</s>, of the nature of bliss,
is unagitated, there is enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>);
when agitated, the authority (<s>adhikāra</s>) of the Lord [manifests];
dissolution (<s>laya</s>) is [the state] that has transcended <s>Bindu</s>.
There is indeed one sole power of consciousness (<s>cit-śakti</s>)
inherent in <s>Śiva</s>;
through the distinction of three kinds of limiting adjuncts,
[she functions as] that of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority.
Through the connection with her,
the one God becomes threefold:
<s>Śiva</s>, <s>Sadāśiva</s>, and the presiding Lord —
possessing dissolution, enjoyment, and authority.
<s>Śakti</s>, consisting of a mass of rays
that are unobstructed and generous,
eternally risen, unlimited,
of <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual) nature,
free from veils, free from dualities,
with splendor that has no material cause,
having transformations that are difficult to arise
through connection with various limiting adjuncts,
most skilled in pervading <s>Bindu</s>
with its quiescent, arisen, and manifold [states],
independent, self-illuminating,
not requiring another, facing all directions,
devoid of beginning, middle, and end,
free from all bonds,
the ultimate, the supreme limit, the transcendent, the subtle —
yearning for the reality alone,
<s>Citi</s> (consciousness) itself is considered the unfading
glory of the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameṣṭhin</s>).
In the proximity of <s>Śiva</s>, who has no previously imposed
distinction whatsoever,
through connection with that very [<s>śakti</s>],
which is of eternal nature due to her specific relation,
<s>Bindu</s> transforms through diverse
<s>vṛttis</s> (modifications), as if concealing [the soul's nature],
filling with sounds the consciousness of the <s>aṇu</s> (bound soul),
which has the luster of <s>cit</s> (consciousness), again and again.
Just as a river, through contact
with the moon in the proximity of the sun,
transforms with trembling
waves, making the sky resound,
this very <s>śakti</s>, abiding in <s>Śiva</s>,
unfailing and possessed of power,
though one and undivided,
is conceived as manifold due to the diversity of effects.
Just as the one power of the sun,
through actions such as giving and taking,
accomplishes the desired even without willing —
such is the imperishable will that is <s>cit</s> (consciousness).
Knowledge, though of the nature of non-knowledge, thus
though actionless, is also action;
whatever effect of hers is known from scripture,
is ascertained by both worlds.
That very <s>śakti</s>, of that very form,
acts with inconceivable splendor.
A single <s>kalpavṛkṣa</s> (wish-fulfilling tree)
grants even many desires.
And the <s>cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-fulfilling gem) [grants] various [wishes],
its glory being inconceivable — likewise,
having a single essential nature without any imposed
distinction or conditioning,
the inconceivable <s>śakti</s> of the all-pervading Lord, which is <s>cit</s> (consciousness),
in accomplishing all purposes,
is neither born nor dies,
neither diminishes nor increases.
<s>Citi</s> (consciousness) is <s>śakti</s> because it is luminous
and because it is non-inert. Moreover, that which
is produced or perishes,
or that which accumulates and diminishes,
that is either of the nature of non-luminosity
or is inert, as is observed —
like the body and such. But she is not so;
therefore this [<s>śakti</s>] does not undergo transformation.
By these two instructions alone,
<s>pariṇāma</s> (real transformation) is refuted.
For transformation of the power of consciousness
into non-consciousness is indeed observed [to be impossible].
Untouched by transformation,
eternal, abiding in <s>Śiva</s>,
through inherence and identity,
<s>cit</s> (consciousness) indeed does not undergo transformation.
This [<s>śakti</s>] is eternal, because she is the cause
of all effects, just as <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is.
Because there is no cause [prior to her] in existence,
she is held to be like <s>Bindu</s>.
For indeed, depending on her,
other [entities] exist, she being eternal;
upon whose establishment the world is established,
and without whose establishment there is nothing.
Whose existence is to be proven,
and by whom or by what is it demonstrated?
Some learned ones proclaim
this [consciousness] to be non-dual.
They [speak of] <s>citi</s> (consciousness), adorned with the play of
<s>vivarta</s> (apparent transformation) in the form of existent and non-existent,
just as a rope produces the illusion
of a snake, a hole, or a garland.
It does not produce those objects;
it merely projects what is non-existent.
Similarly, this [consciousness], being mere knowledge,
appears as one and many through delusion.
This delusion is without support,
contradicting all principles of reasoning.
Since its root is cut upon investigation,
it is not the cause of bondage or liberation.
Therefore there is no bound one, no bondage,
and no binder either, upon investigation.
There exists only the eternally liberated, non-dual, infinite
<s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness) alone.
But how then is even this appearance
of difference perceived?
[They say:] Conventional practice, which is of the nature of difference,
should be understood as like the <s>yakṣa</s> in a banyan tree.
For indeed, the difference of entities
is not perceived by the senses directly, because sense-cognition
is equal to that of infants and mutes,
being non-conceptual and object-produced.
That [perception] determines objects
but does not negate anything.

children.text: Allusion, as Agh points out, to Brahmasiddhi 2:1: āhurvidhātṛ pratyakṣaṃ | na niṣeddhṛ vipaścitaḥ |

children.translated_text: That cognition which involves qualification,
preceded by verbal impressions,
arises through senses dependent on place, time, and such —
that, however, is not
knowledge born of the capacity of the object [itself];
it is considered like memory and conceptual construction.
Neither inference nor scripture are
valid means [of knowledge] there, due to the absence of that [difference].
Perception alone is [the authority] regarding that object;
even those [inference and scripture] are objects of conceptual thought.
Therefore, the confused intellect is bound
by the nooses of doubt arising from itself.
One is released from those very [bonds] —
bondage and liberation are not real.
[The author responds:] Thus those possessed by the demon of <s>Advaita</s> (non-dualism),
babbling [such doctrines], are awakened by compassionate
<s>gurus</s> (teachers)
who bestow the <s>Siddhānta Āgama</s> (established scripture).
If this non-dual <s>saṃvitti</s> (consciousness)
were to be established by empirical
<s>pramāṇas</s> (means of knowledge), by those very [means]
its having-a-second would be firmly [established].
The well-established <s>dharmin</s> (subject), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), and <s>hetu</s> (reason),
which are indeed distinct,
are strengthened by <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion)
for establishing an unestablished property.
An already established property is not proved,
nor is it proved by those [means] that are themselves unestablished.
And establishment and non-establishment combined
cannot reside in a single [locus].
Inference would be a valid means [of knowledge]
when there is difference between the <s>sapakṣa</s> (similar) and <s>pakṣa</s> (dissimilar instances).
For when they are identical, the reason lacks
positive concomitance, due to the absence of that [distinction].
Whose [is the pervasion], with what, and how?
An argument deployed to establish non-duality
actually proclaims difference,
in order to establish its own constituents.
Even negation in the form 'non-dual'
would apply to <s>citi</s> (consciousness) in that view;
thereby the existence of duality elsewhere
would certainly be established, even in [their] proof.
Their thesis is broken,
being a mere expansion of hope.
Scripture too, through its various words,
by virtue of the specific meanings it recalls,
how could it speak of the class of word-meanings
as qualified by relations
if this consciousness were non-dual
and intended to express [only] itself?
How could scripture establish non-duality,
and how could inference do so,
when [these are] being obstructed by their own constituents
that are capable of destroying non-duality?
Moreover, words are seen to abandon
their primary meaning due to contradiction,
and to operate
in a secondary meaning, in both worldly usage and the <s>Vedas</s>.
[Expressions like] 'the ox is a Brāhmaṇa,' 'this is the sun,'
'the sacrificial post' — and so forth.
But a reason does not establish the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved)
when the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) is not observed.
Therefore, scriptural texts about the duality of selves,
compelled by the force of reason,
even abandoning their primary meaning,
make praise of [non-dual] consciousness.
Perception also grasps
the <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual) [knowledge] of an object —
that is, difference from others, the form of exclusion,
by which [determinate knowledge] arises.
The [cognition] that arises, preceded by recollection
of specific [features] such as name and so forth,
<s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate), free from doubt,
devoid of error,
that cognition called perception
cannot be explained otherwise.
For one who has not grasped the difference of the object,
the specific features like name and such [cannot arise].
The fruitfulness of inference too
depends on the apprehension of difference.
In the relation of grasping <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion),
[if there were only] generality, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established.
Moreover, if one admits the otherness
of non-duality and difference,
then difference would be established; or else
non-difference itself would thereby be proved [to be contradictory].
For mere illustration alone
does not establish the thesis. Therefore,
the rope example serves only
to confuse the student.
Nor is the rope comparable to <s>saṃvit</s> (consciousness),
due to the non-apprehension of specific features.
[The rope] appears to transform into those entities
that are removable by mere knowledge.
But she [<s>saṃvit</s>] is known through self-awareness,
and appears to transform into those various entities
for the bound soul (<s>paśu</s>) whose power of vision
is obstructed by <s>mala</s> (impurity), like the moon [appears multiple to one with eye-disease].

body.text: N.B. jalacandra example, again for vivarta

children.translated_text: Just as one with <s>timira</s> (eye-disease),
even reasoning with a thousand arguments,
sees the one moon as many
again and again,
or just as one whose tongue is afflicted by bile,
even reasoning that [milk] is sweet,
perceives even the sweet
milk as bitter, due to the defect of the sense-organ,
or just as when water mixed with collyrium
is being heated,
even for the learned, the perceptions of blue and hot
[arise] due to non-discrimination,
similarly, [consciousness] though properly examined
by <s>āgamas</s> (scriptures) with reasoning,
appears to transform — as 'born,'
'destroyed,' 'manifold,' and so on —
one should understand [this as] non-cessation of knowledge.
The cause is like <s>timira</s> (eye-disease) and such.
That [cause], through meditation on <s>Śiva</s>
and through [the means] taught in the <s>Śiva-śāstra</s>,
can be removed only through [ritual] action,
not otherwise, by millions of cognitions.
Just as eye-disease and such [are cured] through treatment
prescribed in the medical science,
how could there be <s>vivarta</s> (apparent transformation) of <s>citi</s> (consciousness)
that is never otherwise apprehended, even in different places, times, and persons,
and that is uncontradicted
by [any] <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of knowledge)?
Moreover, this world is indeed illusory (<s>māyeya</s>) —
this is established by the <s>pramāṇas</s> themselves.
Therefore, consciousness appears to transform
only due to the bondage of the <s>aṇus</s> (bound souls).
<s>Vivarta</s> (apparent transformation) is indeed of the power of <s>cit</s> (consciousness) —
a false modification by which
even what is not of that nature
is experienced as if it were of that nature.
This [<s>vivarta</s>], mutually connected,
pertaining to both <s>cit</s> (consciousness) and <s>acit</s> (insentient matter),
is accomplished through mutual superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>),
arising from non-discrimination (<s>aviveka</s>).
There, <s>cit</s> (consciousness), due to non-discrimination
from the <s>buddhi-tattva</s> connected with itself,
superimposing upon itself the modifications
of that [<s>buddhi</s>], though itself unchanging,
following births and such — as 'born,'
'destroyed,' 'manifold,'
'with pleasure,' 'with pain' —
displays itself thus to the <s>aṇu</s> (bound soul).
Likewise, the inert [body], superimposing upon itself
the quality of consciousness,
through non-discrimination, knows [itself as conscious].
Therefore, a child [says] 'I am thin' and so forth.
This non-discrimination of all
<s>aṇus</s> (bound souls) is caused by <s>mala</s> (impurity).
[It is] the root-bulb of the stream dominated by delusion,
between consciousness and inert matter.
For the <s>vivarta</s>-distinction of specific
modes of consciousness with specific inert objects
would not be possible
without a firm bond [between them].
For indeed, the 'I'-notion arises in [one's own] body,
not in a clod of earth — and even that [I-notion arises]
only for [that particular] <s>aṇu</s>, not for all.
Therefore bondage between those two is affirmed.
Whichever sense-organs of knowledge and action
belonged to a particular person,
those are not again the instruments
of another; similarly between those two.
Only a specific <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) is prevented
from being the [cause of] <s>vivarta</s> for a [different] specific consciousness.
Not every intellect [serves] all [souls];
hence bondage between those two is affirmed.
Pleasure or pain that has risen in the intellect
is experienced by a certain
person alone through that [particular intellect].
The bond between those two is the determining factor.
If non-discrimination is the determining factor,
then what causes it between those two?
Through that, bondage exists; and bondage
is considered distinct from the Lord.
The deluded self abides in bondage;
<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) is the release from that bondage.
When bondage is entirely dissolved
and the <s>āṇava-mala</s> (innate impurity) is released,
the <s>śakti</s> that illuminates all objects
manifests as that of <s>Śiva</s> alone.
This supreme <s>śakti</s>,
freed from all coverings,
enveloping [only] a limited
range of objects, she reveals.
When there is no bondage
of the <s>śakti</s> whose nature is supreme consciousness,
the supreme alone would shine forth
for the liberated <s>aṇus</s> unceasingly.

children.text: Agh: malarahitatvena svaparaprakāśikāyā muktātmasaṃvidaḥ paramātraṃ parasya vastunaḥ sattāmātraṃ prakāśeta, na tu baddhātmavadasya viśeṣeṇa bhogyatayā prakāśata ityarthaḥ, tathātve muktasyāpi sukhaduḥkhādisaṃvedanena bhoktṛtvaprasaṅgāt

children.translated_text: Therefore, the liberated are omniscient,
not mere knowers of consciousness alone.
If there were an external object, then ignorance
of that object would be caused by darkness (<s>tamas</s>).
For those covered by darkness
are indeed not liberated.
<s>Vikalpa</s> (conceptual thought) arises from the agitation of <s>Bindu</s>,
through the piercing of <s>śabda</s> (word) into the consciousness
of <s>aṇus</s> (bound souls) obstructed by <s>mala</s> (impurity),
in the perception of objects.
For those free from <s>mala</s>, due to the non-agitation
of <s>Bindu</s>, the non-conceptual apprehension of objects,
born from the [release of] that bondage,
is like that of a child born that day.
Whatever entity exists at whatever time,
past or future, then and there,

children.text: syntax of this line unclear; do we have a masculine-neuter switch in the middle?

children.translated_text: the imperishable <s>cit</s> (consciousness), self-cognizing,
grasps the state of the object as it truly is.
They [the liberated souls] are not creators of the universe,
for <s>Śiva</s> alone is its creator.
For there is no evidence anywhere
for a multiplicity of creators.
The eternally liberated, arisen, inconceivable
power called <s>śakti</s>,
which is <s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness), forever takes refuge
in <s>Śiva</s>, the supreme cause.
Through her, pervading the insentient realm,
He creates, preserves, and destroys;
the Lord conceals
and bestows grace upon the souls.
In these [five] acts, He the agent
is taught by the preceptors to be threefold within the five [acts]:
as <s>śaktimān</s> (possessing power), <s>āhitodyoga</s> (with initiated activity),
and <s>pravṛtta</s> (actively engaged).

body.text: Allusion to śaktodyuktaḥ pravṛttaśca kartā trividha iṣyate, which is quoted in KirV 3, ad Mat VP 3:20, and as Śataratnasaṅgraha 14. And note that here too it is attributed to humans with deśikaiḥ.

children.translated_text: There, the first is the capable one,
the partless (<s>niṣkala</s>) one called <s>Śiva</s>.
In him, as if in a bud, rests
the sovereign <s>śakti</s> called <s>kriyā</s> (action).
That very [<s>śakti</s>], when opening forth, having attained
the fullness of <s>Bindu</s> within her womb,
manifests to the Lord on high
the continuous stream of supreme bliss.
With her He eternally delights,
fully engaged — <s>Sadāśiva</s>,
the glorious Lord of the five <s>mantras</s> as his body,
both <s>sakala</s> (with parts) and <s>niṣkala</s> (partless).
Because of contemplation (<s>manana</s>) of all entities
and protection (<s>trāṇa</s>) from the ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
his <s>śakti</s> is indeed of the nature of <s>mantra</s>,
possessing the qualities of contemplation and protection.

body.text: Agh: taduktam---`mananaṃ sarvaveditvaṃ trāṇaṃ saṃsāryanugrahaḥ | mananatrāṇadharmitvānmatra ityabhidhīyate' iti | eṣā ca vyutpattiḥ śivasya śaktervidyeśvarādīnāṃ ca samānaiva, ataśca vācakaśabdānāmupacāreṇa mantraśabdaprayogaḥ

children.translated_text: Due to the diversity of effects and by virtue of
the [different] substrata, though one, she [appears] fivefold.
She shines as <s>Bindu</s>, <s>Śānti</s>, and so forth,
having the five substrata as her domain.
<s>Bindu</s>, <s>Śānti</s>, <s>Kalā</s>, <s>Vidyā</s>,
<s>Pratiṣṭhā</s>, together with <s>Nivṛtti</s> —
these five are the loci of experience;
their collective designation as <s>Bindu</s> is proclaimed by <s>Śiva</s>.
This undivided [totality] of the five
<s>kalās</s> is designated as <s>Bindu</s>.
The supreme form pertains to that [<s>Bindu</s>];
the lower form pertains to effects.
That pure <s>śakti</s> of <s>Śiva</s>
which is inherent [in him],
that very form, due to the division of actions,
is called the body named <s>Sadākhya</s>.
<s>Mahāmāyā</s>, pervaded
by the powerful <s>Śiva</s>,
for the pure souls (<s>śivātmans</s>)
established in the loci of experience,
produces bodies, enjoyments, sense-organs, planes,
and cognition and so forth.
That is her effect; she is the <s>kriyāśakti</s> (power of action),
and is also so called.
The one <s>śakti</s> of the Trident-bearer (<s>Śūlin</s>), having the nature
of all knowledge and action,

children.text: QUOTATION of Moksa 25cd: sarvajñānakriyārūpā śaktirekaiva śūlinaḥ

children.translated_text: the powers beginning with will, knowledge, and action,
are the sources of effects.
For the <s>Īśvaras</s> and <s>Śivas</s>,
the bodies, senses, and so forth, which are made of <s>Mahāmāyā</s>,
are pure,
auspicious, and suited to their respective domains.
This <s>śakti</s>, whose essence is action,
is inseparable from <s>Śiva</s>.
Due to that connection, <s>Śiva</s> is called the cause
of all effects
without exception.
He, descending from <s>bindu</s>, atomic,
enveloped by <s>Sadāśiva</s>,
to the offices of lordly functions,
[dispatching] <s>Sadāśivas</s> and <s>Maheśvaras</s>,
sending [them] forth, at the summit of all paths,
the Lord shines.
Having five streams as faces, peaceful,
the Lord, with <s>Śakti</s> as his head — <s>Śiva</s>;
with large eyes [representing] seeing, action, and will,
endowed with the crescent moon of <s>vijñāna</s> (knowledge),
with <s>Īśāna</s> as the crown, <s>Puruṣa</s> as the face,
with a circle of arms [extending to] the ten directions;
<s>Aghora</s> as the heart, <s>Vāma</s>
as the secret [part], radiant with a body born [of the five mantras],
this God, being active,
complete (<s>sakala</s>), all-purifying.

body.text:
NOTE that this is the end of the commentary on the half-verse śaktodyuktaḥ pravṛttaśca kartā trividha iṣyate, which was allued to in 265.
NOTE also that these last two verses could be considered to be a paraphrase of Parakhya 2:84--85b or of Mat VP 4:14c--15b.

children.translated_text: <s>Śiva</s> is indeed one; likewise,
<s>Śakti</s> too is without modification;
in the [three states of] dissolution, enjoyment, and authority,
those two are of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
Indeed, in the pure, noble,
and deep ocean of consciousness,
some, established by him,
dissolve in their own Self.
Others, their own powers restrained
by <s>Śiva</s>, repose [in dissolution].
Others, embracing <s>Mahāmāyā</s>,
which is active —
their minds focused solely on the bliss of contact with her,
intent on enjoyment.
Likewise, others, taking shelter in the supreme sky (<s>paravyoman</s>),
at the summit of the paths,
perform the five functions,
following the command of the Lord.
Therefore, he, though being one among those
who partake of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority,
assumes differentiation through the role of presider —
[a differentiation that is] figurative.
Similarly, <s>Śakti</s> is regarded [as one];
the differentiation of those two is now explained.
In the pure path, <s>Śiva</s> is the agent;
<s>Śakti</s>, the instrument, is the one relied upon.
He should be known as the support [of all],
self-established, of dense consciousness.
She is <s>Saṃvid</s> (awareness), whose arising
is [characterized by] eagerness in the apprehension of all objects;
and she is of the nature of supreme sovereignty,
[his] glory, having the form of pervasion.
This great <s>Maheśvara</s> (Great Lord),
the pervader of all objects, [is known] through those two [aspects].
That form which is independent of anything external —
that knowledge is designated <s>Śiva</s>.
The wise declare his <s>Śakti</s> to be
the form that depends on the external.
The awareness of every entity whatsoever
has two aspects;
through that which depends on the external and that which is independent —
<s>Śakti</s> exists, having <s>Śiva</s> as her ground.
For <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), whose glory is eternally manifest
and unlimited,
with respect to objects to be known, things to be presided over, effects, and so on —
nothing other [than <s>Śakti</s>], such as auxiliary causes, [is needed].
Therefore, <s>Śakti</s> — the form that depends on the external —
befits the Lord.
The externally-dependent form alone
is not sufficient for everyone [to produce effects],
since effects such as sons and the like
are observed [to arise] only otherwise [i.e., through instruments].
Knowledge is never without an object;
it is indeed the grasping of objects.
Whether through opposition or in sequence —
even so, that which is imperishable,
this is the characteristic of perishable [cognitions]:
that which does not arise otherwise at that time.
That which is imperishable is eternal —
this is accepted; from this, [<s>Śakti</s>] differs.
<s>Śakti</s> belongs to <s>Śambhu</s> by way of substrate;
and he to her — likewise.
The designation '<s>Śakti</s>' may apply to the dense consciousness
due to the conditioning adjunct of effects;
but <s>Śakti</s> as externally-dependent
does not truly exist — so say some.
That an agent could produce effects
without an instrument —
this view of theirs is unjustified,
being contradicted by both reasoning and direct perception.
Moreover, even if the effect of the Lord
were accepted as a conditioning adjunct,
since he would always be in a conditioned state,
how could <s>Śiva</s> be unconditioned?
And how could he be an agent
devoid of knowledge of the instrument?
Or how could <s>Puruṣa</s> (the soul)
perceive <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect) without that <s>Śakti</s>?
This [world] would be utter darkness
without the lamp of <s>Śakti</s>.
It would become something else; and the Lord,
being powerless, what could he do?
Though non-different from <s>Śambhu</s>,
<s>Śakti</s> is accepted as distinct.
Just as a lentil from its husk —
neither separate, for the reasons stated;

children.translated_text: though non-different, yet distinct —
she is inherent in <s>Śambhu</s>,
natural and rooted in him,
like the radiance of the sun, spotless.
For this Lord, by a <s>Śakti</s>
that is utterly different from his own self,
never creates anything,
nor ever knows anything.
Though without imposed distinctions,
the deity <s>Maheśvara</s> is the cause.
The differentiation of effects too
would arise from the particular states of the effect.
<s>Bindu</s>, whose effects have dissolved,
impelled by <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Śakti</s>,
for creation, for maintenance,
of the creator, and for the dissolution of the manifest world —
having maintained the universe for a long time,
<s>bindu</s> alone sets [all] in motion.
Just as, having arrived at a different state,
[clay] begins [to form] a pot —
through clay's transition to another state —
so too, as before, this [<s>bindu</s>],
pervaded by the Lord's <s>Śakti</s>,
through the particular functions in each [stage],
is equipped for the differentiation of effects,
even though the Trident-bearer (<s>Śūlin</s>) is without modification.
Though himself unchanged,
[<s>Śiva</s> is the cause] of the states that arise in due sequence —
splitting, desiccation, and pulverization —
which are born from difference of states.
Just as the sun with its hot rays
is the maker of the lotus [opening, closing, etc.], so <s>Śiva</s>,
the creator of effects such as creation and so forth,
[is] unchanged yet possessed of <s>Śakti</s>.
Just as with beeswax and clay,
without dependence [on anything else] and instantaneously,
the sun is the cause of liquidity and dryness,
though itself unchanged —
so too, [for] the atoms (<s>aṇus</s>) possessing equal and unequal
actions called merit and demerit,
<s>Śiva</s>, though himself unchanged,
is the agent of bondage and liberation.
When two <s>karmas</s> that have mutually obstructed
each other's fruition
come together, <s>Śiva</s>'s <s>Śakti</s>
descends upon the soul (<s>aṇu</s>).

body.text: A plain affirmation, in spite of what Agh's commentary may say, of the karmasāmyapakṣa (not the malaparipākapakṣa).

children.translated_text: The moment that [<s>Śakti</s>] has descended,
the dense covering is shaken off;
with the turbidity of <s>mala</s> (impurity) pacified,
[the soul] perceives itself.
Truly at that very moment, he is liberated,
when touched by <s>Śiva</s>'s will.
Through perpetual and occasional
<s>karma</s> (ritual action) alone, he henceforth continues.
With this very body,
the supreme, unbroken pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>),
the greatly steadfast and blessed
<s>Śiva-yogins</s> attain.
He purifies by his glance, by his speech,
by his feet, and by his hand —
rivers, towns, gardens,
cities, and other [places], through his mere sport.
How much more then this person
who, terrified of worldly existence, has come for refuge!
Salutation to such a one — our
<s>Guru</s> (teacher), who is the radiance of <s>Śiva</s>,
the treasure-house of the gems of <s>yoga</s>
that bestow infinite fruit.
By one whose mind was purified through the illumination
composed by <s>Rāmakaṇṭha</s>,
this <s>Ratnatrayaparīkṣā</s> (Examination of the Three Jewels)
was composed by the learned <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s>,
following the excellent commentary (<s>vṛtti</s>)
of the venerable <s>Rāmakaṇṭha</s>.
The meaning of the <s>Ratnatrayaparīkṣā</s>
has been illuminated in brief.
